name: Ob-Ugric
region: The Ob and Irtysh basins of western Siberia
defining_innovation: Khanty and Mansi, the Siberian relatives of Hungarian, grouped by their shared vocabulary and neighbouring territory. Whether they form a true subgroup of their own is debated.

chapters.title: Origins
chapters.body:
Khanty and Mansi are spoken by small communities of fishers, hunters and reindeer herders along the Ob and its tributaries. They are Hungarian's closest living relatives, although the connection has become hard to see after nearly three thousand years apart. Each is really a cluster of very different dialects: the eastern and northern varieties of Khanty are barely mutually intelligible.

The two languages share a good deal of vocabulary and grammar, partly inherited and partly the result of centuries as neighbours, and they are traditionally grouped as 'Ob-Ugric'. Some specialists argue that the shared features are mostly the result of contact.

chapters.title: Under Russian Rule
chapters.body: Russian conquest of western Siberia began in the 1580s, followed by tribute, Christianisation and settlement. Soviet language policy gave Khanty and Mansi Latin-based alphabets in the early 1930s, replaced them with Cyrillic in 1937, and then promoted Russian in schools. The discovery of oil and gas in the region from the 1960s brought mass immigration, and Khanty and Mansi are now small minorities in the Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug named after them. The southern dialects of both languages died out in the 20th century.

speakers.note: Mostly Khanty; Mansi had fewer than a thousand speakers in the 2010 census. Every variety is endangered, most severely so, and the southern dialects of both are extinct.

sources.citation: Rosstat. 2012. Itogi Vserossiyskoy perepisi naseleniya 2010 goda [Results of the All-Russian Population Census 2010], vol. 4: national composition and languages.
Moseley, Christopher, ed. 2010. Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger, 3rd ed. Paris: UNESCO Publishing.
Eberhard, David M., Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig, eds. 2024. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 27th ed. Dallas: SIL International.

turning_points.title: Khanty and Mansi diverge
turning_points.description: Khanty and Mansi develop separately along different stretches of the Ob and its tributaries. Whether they first shared a common Ob-Ugric stage after leaving Hungarian behind is disputed.

sources.citation: Bakró-Nagy, Marianne, Johanna Laakso & Elena Skribnik, eds. 2022. The Oxford Guide to the Uralic Languages. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

turning_points.title: Russian conquest of Siberia
turning_points.description: Russian forts, tribute collection and missions reach the Ob. Russian loans and, in places, a shift to Russian follow, along with contact with Komi and Tatar traders and settlers.

sources.citation: Abondolo, Daniel, ed. 1998. The Uralic Languages. London: Routledge.

turning_points.title: Soviet alphabets
turning_points.description: Khanty and Mansi receive Latin-based alphabets under the Soviet programme for northern peoples, which are replaced by Cyrillic from 1937. With so many different dialects, no single written standard fits all speakers.

sources.citation: Bakró-Nagy, Marianne, Johanna Laakso & Elena Skribnik, eds. 2022. The Oxford Guide to the Uralic Languages. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

turning_points.title: Southern dialects disappear
turning_points.description: The southern varieties of Mansi and Khanty, closest to Russian and Tatar settlement, lose their last speakers. Their exact end dates are poorly recorded.

sources.citation: Bakró-Nagy, Marianne, Johanna Laakso & Elena Skribnik, eds. 2022. The Oxford Guide to the Uralic Languages. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

turning_points.title: Oil, gas and immigration
turning_points.description: Oil and gas production in western Siberia brings hundreds of thousands of Russian-speaking settlers. Khanty and Mansi become small minorities in their homeland, and most children now grow up speaking Russian.

sources.citation: Bakró-Nagy, Marianne, Johanna Laakso & Elena Skribnik, eds. 2022. The Oxford Guide to the Uralic Languages. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
